newsitem.title: USA: Cosby family thanks witnesses for helping police.
newsitem.headline: Cosby family thanks witnesses for helping police.

text.p: Bill Cosby and his family expressed their gratitude Saturday to witnesses and others who have helped police gather clues and put together a composite sketch of the man suspected of killing the entertainer's son.

"The Cosby family extends their hearts and deep appreciation to those who have come forward to help lighten the load of the Los Angeles Police Department," they said in a statement released by Cosby's publicist, David Brokaw.

Police Saturday released a drawing of a white male suspect, 25 to 32 years old and wearing a light-coloured knit cap, and asked for the public's aid in bringing him to justice. The sketch was made with the help of a woman who witnessed part of the attack on 27-year-old Ennis Cosby.
Speaking from a secret location in the East where the family has secluded itself to mourn their loss, the famed actor-comedian told Brokaw he was struggling to cope with personal tragedy.
"Your concentration goes in 18 different directions," Cosby told his longtime spokesman. "You try to pull things back together but it's like playing with oil and water."

But Brokaw said that even while grieving, Cosby had taken time to speak by phone to the mother of a 17-year-old girl who was killed by an armed gang member while riding a city bus in Los Angeles last Thursday.
The murder of Corie Williams, a high school senior, came only hours after the younger Cosby was killed by an unidentified gunman while changing a tire along a southern California freeway.

But Cosby, who in a written statement Friday blasted the news media for staking out the family's homes, also said he found it "regrettable" that television news crews had gathered on the doorstep of the slain girl's mother.
"They're standing there asking questions that have nothing to do with the person she just lost," Cosby was quoted as saying.

In a message left on his publicist's answering machine, Cosby challenged news organisations that specialise in celebrity-oriented "tabloid" journalism to offer a reward for information on the killer instead of using their money to buy exclusives.

"It's the tabloids," Cosby said. "They're looking for something and they pay money for pictures. They pay money to have witnesses talk and it disrupts the case. Why can't the tabloids put out the word ... that they would pay to have someone come forward and they could have exclusivity of the story."
